problem: Adapting a real-time object detector to a new environment requires both robot navigation to collect images and human annotation. Prior embodied active learning either assumes whole trajectories are annotated or uses non-embodied active learning, so neither budget is handled jointly.
motivation: Detectors suffer from domain shift in new environments, and detection errors are a common failure in object search and instruction following. Annotation and navigation time are both scarce, so the agent must go to error-prone places and annotate only the most informative frames. Inconsistent predictions of the same objects across consecutive views can reveal errors without labels.
key_idea: Use a label-free Prediction Discrepancy score (mismatch of detected classes in the overlapping region of consecutive frames) to guide both a Bayesian-optimization navigation agent and a difficulty-plus-diversity selection of frames for annotation.
insight: Discrepancy-selected samples are harder for the model (lowest F1 on annotated samples: 67.26 in sim, 39.63 real, vs 77.78 / 46.08 for Random) and more class-balanced (class entropy 3.96 vs 3.78 for Random) with fewer object annotations than Count/Entropy. So the score finds the model's weak classes, approaching the Oracle-like class-difficulty selection without labels. The navigation ablation shows that steering the agent with the same score beats FBE, Sweep and Random walk over the long run.
method: Task formulation: embodied batch active learning with R rounds, each with T navigation steps to fill a collection buffer and A annotations, followed by retraining from the initial weights on all accumulated annotations.

Prediction Discrepancy: size of the symmetric difference (multiset, class-matched) between the classes detected in consecutive frames restricted to their overlapping region R(a); small or border objects are ignored; a frame's score is the average over visited neighbor pairs. R is estimated from the action in sim and by homography + RANSAC in the real world.

Adaptive navigation agent: path-aware BO with a Random Forest surrogate of state -> discrepancy and UCB (mu+3sigma); the acquisition is the mean UCB along the shortest path; the best of 50 random destinations is chosen; weighted A* uses cost (1-normalized UCB)/2 for unvisited states and 1 for visited ones.

Data selection: PPAL-style two-stage selection. Take the top 3A frames by discrepancy, then cluster with CCMS on frozen ResNet features into A clusters. Annotated frames are added to the clustering and their clusters are discarded to avoid redundancy.
Baselines for scoring/navigation: Count, Entropy, Oracle (GT per-class AP gap) and Random scoring; FBE, Sweep and Random-walk agents.

Real-world pipeline: Spot robot with YOLOv5; stored trajectories are scored by summed acquisition values and the best is chosen; OWLv2 pre-labels images and a human corrects them (about 4.5 s per image).

setting.backbone: YOLOv5 S/M/L (fine-tuned each round; COCO weights then pretrained on scene data); ResNet features for clustering; Random Forest surrogate; OWLv2 as labeling oracle in the real world
setting.training_data: COCO-pretrained YOLOv5, pretrained on 100 random images in each of the first 64 ProcTHOR houses (real: 100 images in the scene); adapted with 20 annotations per round for 10 rounds (sim) or 5 rounds (real)
setting.action_space: discrete grid: move 25 cm in 4 directions, rotate 45°, look up/down 30° (sim); Spot: 0.15 m steps, 10° yaw, 3 body heights, sit/stand/crouch (real)
setting.simulator: AI2-THOR / ProcTHOR (90 houses; adaptation on the last 10) plus real world
setting.privileged: Oracle annotator (simulator GT labels or OWLv2 + human correction) for the selected frames; the Oracle scoring baseline also uses GT, but the main method does not

numbers_note: Detection mAP50 results are given only as figures (IQM curves), so no table numbers; the only tables are annotated-data characteristics, which are not navigation metrics.
results: In ProcTHOR (10 scenes x 10 seeds) and on a Spot robot (15 seeds), Prediction Discrepancy scoring beats Entropy, Count and Random in mAP50 under equal budgets. Only the GT-based Oracle is better. The Adaptive BO agent beats FBE, Sweep and Random walk in the long run. The real-world gain over Random is smaller because the scene is a single room with a smaller budget.
limitations: Discrepancy ignores localization errors and uses only class-level matching; the overlap is heuristic in sim, and a homography in the real world requires enough features.
Evaluated on the same scene used for adaptation, on a single small real room; the Oracle remains better; results appear only as figures without numeric tables.
Real-world data is pre-recorded trajectories chosen by score, not online closed-loop navigation, and labeling relies on a slow foundation model plus human correction.
builds_on: Semantic Curiosity for Active Visual Learning (Chaplot et al.)
Zheng et al. (Towards Optimal Pretraining for embodied detectors)
